source.title: Root Defense Strategies: Ensuring Safety of LLM at the Decoding Level
source.authors: Xin-Yi Zeng; Yuying Shang; Jiawei Chen; Jingyuan Zhang; Yu Tian

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some table formatting is flattened, but the relevant pilot finding is stated in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies token-level harmfulness classification and proposes a decoding defense, but does not test the listed fine-tuning, aligned-versus-base KL, bypass, parameter-localization, or safety-deepening claims.
record.gate_note: The pilot study reports that a classifier can distinguish harmful and benign decoding to some degree, but this is not a measurement of aligned-versus-base per-token KL or of safety behavior being localized to early positions. The reported RDS defense outcomes compare the paper's own new defense with other methods; they do not test whether the bypass mechanisms in the claim defeat safety. The paper's cited claims are not recorded as its own results.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a decoding-level defense (RDS) and a pilot hidden-state classifier visualization. It runs no harmful or benign fine-tuning, no aligned-vs-base per-token KL, no bypass attack (prefill, suffix, decoding) measured as a rate, no parameter localization, and no training-based deepening. RDS is a mitigation, and its Table 1 results compare the paper's own method with baselines. The text mentions a 'reject first then answer' pattern under random sampling only qualitatively, with no rate, and cites Zhou et al. for deepening rather than testing it.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that LLMs can discern the harmfulness of output tokens across decoding steps. They also conclude that RDS, a step-by-step classifier-guided token reranking with speculative decoding, improves safety and speed without substantially hurting utility.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes a decoder-level token-filtering defense; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or KL-measurement methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports weaker classifier AUC on Xstest (0.65–0.89) than on Custom (1.00) and the other listed datasets (0.99–1.00), but this is a classifier result rather than a test of the claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: For harmful queries, a PCA-based linear classifier on top-layer hidden states places refusal tokens closer to the harmful side than compliant tokens, across output positions 1–8. Hard classification is poor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model hidden states during decoding carry a graded harmfulness signal for early output tokens that can steer token selection.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The pilot experiment samples one output per query; the paper says hard classification performs poorly, and the token-position results are mainly presented in figures without numerical per-model values. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and other comparisons of RDS with baselines are performance results for the paper's newly proposed defense, not tests of the claim's bypass mechanisms or listed training and localization claims. Cited results from other work are also excluded.

untested.parts: No aligned-vs-base per-token KL or position-wise divergence.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attack. The 'reject first then answer' sampling pattern is noted only qualitatively.
No analysis of the data or objective causing shallowness.
RDS is an inference-time decoding defense, not training that deepens alignment. Its robustness to prefill or fine-tuning attacks is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: Table 1 RDS-vs-baseline compliance and refusal rates, and Table 4 initial model compliance on Custom, are defense or baseline results, not tests of any version. Exclusion is correctly declared in rows_left_out. The paper cites Qi et al. 2023 (an original source) only as a benchmark source (HEx-PHI).

versions.untested_parts: No test of compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes used to bypass refusal.
No test of whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
No test of whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
RDS is a decoding defense, not a training method that spreads safety beyond early tokens; persistence of deepened safety is not tested.

rows.subject: Five evaluated LLMs (collective description: Llama-2-chat-7B, Llama-3-8b-Instruct, Qwen2-7B-Instruct, Vicuna-7B-v1.3, Vicuna-13B-v1.3)
rows.size_stated: 7B, 8B, and 13B, as included in the model names
rows.operation_detail: Classifier assessment of hidden states from generated tokens, comparing harmful and benign output categories.
rows.measure: Classifier score/distribution differentiation between harmful and benign output tokens
rows.value: The text reports that almost all tokens for benign queries remain on the benign side; for harmful queries, some refusal tokens remain on the harmful side while compliant tokens remain on the benign side. Benign tokens from harmful queries are closer to the harmful side than harmful tokens from those queries.
rows.note: The paper describes this collectively; it does not provide numerical per-model results in the text. This is token-classifier separability, not a measure of safety localization or aligned-versus-base KL.
rows.check: Linkage and state are correct. This is hidden-state classifier separability of output tokens at positions 1–8. It does not measure aligned-vs-base KL (V3) or bypass rates (V4). It is a related construct and belongs under fits_no_version. No per-model numbers are given, only figures.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
